## Learning objectives 

<div style="font-size: 130%;">

1. Describe how changing sample size impacts the distribution of the sample mean

2. Explain how the Central Limit Theorem quantifies the uncertainty of a sample mean

</div>

# Question: what is the average daily caffeine consumption among Americans? 

::: {.notes}
CLT: fundamental to the field of statistics, underpins parametric methods including regression, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals.
Allows us to use a sample to make statements/learn about a population

We're going to "discover" the central limit theorem through an example/activity using caffeine consumption. 

Assume familiarity with concepts of mean, variance, distribution, Normal distribution
::: 

# How might we answer this question? 

# We could survey every single American 

::: {.notes}
But this is impractical (impossible?) and expensive
:::

# We could take a sample 

::: {.notes}
Have person 1 take a sample
We're going to pretend that I have all of the data on the entire population, so we can take samples like this. 
::: 


---

### Sample one person 


```{r s1}
#| cache: true 


set.seed(123)
s1 = caffeine_df %>% 
  slice_sample(n=1)

s1 %>% 
  gt() %>% 
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(40),
    heading.title.font.size = px(50),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
    table.align = "left",
    table.width = pct(70),
    quarto.use_bootstrap = TRUE
  ) %>% 
  cols_align("left",
             columns = everything()) %>% 
  cols_label("id" = "Participant ID",
             "age" = "Age (years)",
             "caffeine_mg" = "Caffeine intake (mg)")
```


---

### Add another person to sample and calculate average


```{r s2}
#| cache: true
set.seed(1234)
s2 = caffeine_df %>% 
  slice_sample(n=1)

s1 %>% 
  bind_rows(s2) %>% 
  mutate(cumulative_sample_mean = cummean(caffeine_mg)) %>% 
  gt() %>% 
  fmt_number(columns = cumulative_sample_mean, decimals = 0) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(40),
    heading.title.font.size = px(50),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
    table.align = "left",
    table.width = pct(100)
  ) %>% 
  cols_align("left",
             columns = everything()) %>% 
  cols_label("id" = "Participant ID",
             "age" = "Age (years)",
             "caffeine_mg" = "Caffeine intake (mg)",
             "cumulative_sample_mean" = "Sample mean (cumulative)")
```

### Lily's sample

```{r s4}
#| cache: true
samp_df = 
  s1 %>% 
  bind_rows(s2) %>% 
  bind_rows(s3) %>% 
  mutate(cumulative_sample_mean = cummean(caffeine_mg)) %>% 
  mutate(n = row_number())

samp_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = cumulative_sample_mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 225)) +
  labs(x = "Number of people in sample", y = "Sample mean caffeine (mg)", title = "n = 30")


```

```{r caffeine diagram}
#| cache: true 

# 1. SETUP DATA
# Replace these URLs with your local file paths! 
# e.g., image = c("figs/espresso.jpg", "figs/soda.jpg", ...)
caffeine_data = tibble(
  beverage = c("Monster Java\n(16oz)\n300 mg", "Coca Cola\n(12oz)\n35 mg", "Starbucks Blonde\n(16oz)\n315 mg", "Starbucks Latte\n(16oz)\n150 mg", "Starbucks Matcha\n(16oz)\n65 mg", "Kombucha\n(16oz)\n68 mg", "Herbal Tea\n0 mg", "Home coffee\n(8oz)\n110mg"),
  caffeine_mg = c(300, 35, 315, 150, 65, 68, 0, 100),
  # Using reliable placeholder icons for the demo
  image = c(here::here("docs/figs/monster.jpeg"),
            here::here("docs/figs/coke.jpeg"),
            here::here("docs/figs/grande.jpeg"),
            here::here("docs/figs/latte.jpeg"),
            here::here("docs/figs/matcha.jpeg"),
            here::here("docs/figs/kombucha.png"),
            here::here("docs/figs/herbal.jpeg"),
            here::here("docs/figs/home_coffee.jpeg"))
)

# 2. PREP: Reorder the beverage factor by caffeine amount
plot_data = caffeine_data %>% 
  mutate(beverage = fct_reorder(beverage, caffeine_mg))

# 3. PLOT
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = beverage, y = caffeine_mg)) +
  
  # A. The "Stick" (Lollipop stem)
  geom_segment(aes(xend = beverage, yend = 0), 
               color = "#C4A484", # A nice 'coffee' brown
               linewidth = 1.2, 
               linetype = "dotted") +
  
  # B. The Image (The "Pop")
  geom_image(aes(image = image), size = 0.25) + # Adjust size (0.05 to 0.15 usually good)
  
  # C. The Text Label (Caffeine amount below or above)
  # geom_text(aes(y = 0, label = paste0(caffeine_mg, " mg")),
  #           vjust = 0, # Push text up above the image
  #           color = "#444444",
  #           # fontface = "bold",
  #           size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 400), expand = c(0,0)) + # Give room for the labels
  labs(title = "Caffeine Content by Beverage",
       y = "Caffeine (mg)", 
       x = "") +
  # theme_minimal(base_family = "Source Sans Pro") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), # Remove vertical grid lines
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12, color = "#444444"),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(), # Hide Y axis numbers (since we have labels)
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 20, face = "bold", color = "#6F4E37")
  )
```

### How do the samples compare? 


```{r samp compare}
#| cache: true

samps_df = 
  samp_df2 %>% 
  mutate(name = "Lily's Sample") %>% 
  bind_rows(samp_df_new %>% mutate(name = "Professor 2's Sample")) %>%
  bind_rows(samp_df_again %>% mutate(name = "Professor 3's Sample")) 

samps_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x= n, y = cumulative_sample_mean, color = name)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Number of people in sample", y = "Sample mean caffeine (mg)",
       title = "3 different samples of size n = 100") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,225), breaks = seq(0,225,25)) +
  theme_sub_legend(position = "bottom",
                   text = element_text(size=14),
                   title = element_blank()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#CC79A7","#009E73" ,"#0072B2"))

```



# What will happen if 100 different people take samples?

```{r 100 samples}
#| cache: true

n_sims = 100
generated_df = 
  map_dfr(.x = 1:n_sims,
          .f = function(sim){
            set.seed(sim + 1232)
            df = caffeine_df %>% 
              slice_sample(n=100) %>% 
              mutate(cumulative_sample_mean = cummean(caffeine_mg),
                     n = row_number(),
                     name = sim)

  ggplot() +
   geom_line(data = generated_df, aes(x = n, y = cumulative_sample_mean, group = name),

       title = "100 different samples of size n = 100") +
```

# But there's still some variability

::: {.notes}
If I only have one sample, how do I know if it's "correct"? 
We're not interested in tail behavior, I want to know what is happening *now* 
::: 


---


```{r zoom in 2}
#| cache: true 


p1 +
  geom_labelhline(aes(yintercept = mean(caffeine_df$caffeine_mg)), color = "#E69F00", 
                  label = glue::glue("Population mean = {round(mean(caffeine_df$caffeine_mg), 0)} mg")) +
  geom_point(data = generated_df_big %>% filter(n==100),
             aes(x = n, y = cumulative_sample_mean),
             color = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.5) +

           label = "Let's look at all the sample means where n = 100",
```

---

### Distribution of sample means at  n = 100

```{r dist at 100}

vals = samps_df %>% 
  filter(n == 100) %>% 
  pull(cumulative_sample_mean)
#       id   age caffeine_mg cumulative_sample_mean     n name                
#    <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>                  <dbl> <int> <chr>               
# 1 137545    59        39.3                   68.6   100 Lily's Sample       
# 2 135234     4         1                    120.    100 Professor 2's Sample
# 3 139390     8         4                     95.9   100 Professor 3's Sample
generated_df_big %>% filter(n==100) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = cumulative_sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", binwidth = 10, fill = "#444444")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(5, 200, 10)) +
  annotate(geom = "point", x = vals[1], y = 0, color = "#CC79A7", size = 4) +
  annotate(geom = "point", x = vals[2], y = 0, color = "#009E73", size = 4) +
    annotate(geom = "point", x = vals[3], y = 0, size = 4, color = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = "Sample mean caffeine (mg)", y = "Count")

```

::: {.notes}
Centered around our population mean
Bell curve
For samples of size 100, the sample means are clustered around the population mean, and have this specific shape 
Use this to figure out how far our sample mean is from the truth 
::: 

---

### Distribution of sample means at  n = 100

```{r dist at 100 w normal}
#| cache: true 

sim_mean = mean(generated_df_big %>% filter(n==100) %>% pull(cumulative_sample_mean))
sim_sd = sd(generated_df_big %>% filter(n==100) %>% pull(cumulative_sample_mean))

hist_plot = generated_df_big %>% 
  filter(n==100) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = cumulative_sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), 
                 color = "black", binwidth = 10, fill = "#444444") +
  # 2. Theoretical Normal Curve
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = sim_mean, sd = sim_sd),color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(5, 200, 10)) +
  # 3. The Specific Samples
  annotate(geom = "point", x = vals[1], y = 0, color = "#CC79A7", size = 5) +
  annotate(geom = "point", x = vals[2], y = 0, color = "#009E73", size = 5) +
  annotate(geom = "point", x = vals[3], y = 0, size = 5, color = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = "Sample mean caffeine (mg)", y = "Density")

hist_plot
```

# Let's compare the distribution of sample means for a range of sample sizes


---

```{ojs}
data = FileAttachment("caffeine_df.csv").csv({ typed: true })

<!-- viewof sample_size = Inputs.range( -->
<!--   [2, 120],  -->
<!--   {value: 2, step: 1, label: "Sample size:"} -->
<!-- ) -->

sample_values = [2, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 200, 500]

viewof sample_index = Inputs.range(
  [0, sample_values.length - 1], // Slide from index 0 to 7
  {
    value: 0, // 
    step: 1, 
    label: "Sample size:",
    // This makes the label show "50" instead of "3"
    format: i => sample_values[i] 
  }
)

sample_size = sample_values[sample_index]


sample_means = {
  // Dependency tracking: re-run when these change
  sample_size;
  
  // Safety check: ensure data is loaded
  if (!data || data.length === 0) return [];
  
  // Safety check: ensure column exists (Case Sensitive!)
  if (typeof data[0].caffeine_mg === "undefined") {
    return ["Error: Column 'caffeine_mg' not found in data"];
  }

  const means = [];
  // Create a local copy of the array to shuffle
  // We do this inside the loop or use a specific shuffler to ensure 
  // we are sampling from the full population every time.
  const popArray = Array.from(data); 

  for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) {
    // 1. Shuffle a clean copy of the population
    // 2. Slice the first n elements (Sampling WITHOUT replacement)
    const sample = d3.shuffle([...popArray]).slice(0, sample_size);

    // 3. Compute mean
    const m = d3.mean(sample, d => d.caffeine_mg);
    means.push(m);
  }

  return means;
}


// 5. CALCULATE NORMAL CURVE (THEORETICAL)
// We now generate the curve based on the Population Parameters, not the sample.
// This shows the Theoretical prediction of the CLT.
normalCurve = {
  if (sample_means.length < 2 || !data) return [];
  
  // 1. Get Population Statistics
  const popMean = d3.mean(data, d => d.caffeine_mg);
  const popSD = d3.deviation(data, d => d.caffeine_mg);
  
  // 2. Calculate Standard Error (The predicted width of the sampling distribution)
  // Formula: Population SD / sqrt(n)
  const se = popSD / Math.sqrt(sample_size);

  // 3. Determine range for the curve (centered on popMean)
  const minX = popMean - (4 * se);
  const maxX = popMean + (4 * se);
  
  // Create a smooth grid of X values
  const grid = d3.range(minX, maxX, (maxX - minX) / 200);
  
  // Normal Density Function using Population Mean and Standard Error
  const pdf = (x) => (1 / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))) * Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - popMean) / se, 2));
  
  return grid.map(x => ({x: x, y: pdf(x)}));
}

// 6. PLOT
// 6. SIDE-BY-SIDE PLOTS WITH EXTERNAL LEGEND
{
  // --- A. SETUP VARIABLES ---
  const popMean = d3.mean(data, d => d.caffeine_mg);
  const n = sample_means.length;
  const bins = d3.bin().thresholds(20)(sample_means);
  
  // NEW: Calculate fixed x-axis limits based on the Population Data
  // This ensures the axis stays constant regardless of sample size
  const xLimits = d3.extent(data, d => d.caffeine_mg);
  const xLimits2 = [0, 750];

  // Define colors
  const colorDomain = ["Sampling Distribution Mean", "Population Mean", "Normal Curve"];
  const colorRange = ["black", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"];

  // --- B. POPULATION PLOT (Left) ---
  const popPlot = Plot.plot({
    width: 550,
    height: 500,
    caption: "Population Distribution (Raw Data)",
    marginTop: 40,
    marginLeft: 50,
    marginBottom: 40,
    style: { fontSize: "14px", overflow: "visible" },
    
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(data, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "caffeine_mg", fill: "#444444", fillOpacity: 0.5})),
    ],
    // We explicitly set the domain here too, just to be safe and consistent
    x: { label: "Caffeine consumption (mg)", domain: xLimits }, 
    y: { label: "Count" }
  });

  // --- C. SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION PLOT (Right) ---
  const sampPlot = Plot.plot({
    width: 550,
    height: 500,
    caption: `Distribution of sample means at (n=${sample_size})`,
    marginTop: 40,
    marginLeft: 50,
    marginBottom: 40,
    style: { fontSize: "14px", overflow: "visible" },
    
    color: {
      domain: colorDomain,
      range: colorRange,
      legend: false
    },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(bins, {
        x1: "x0", x2: "x1", 
        y: d => d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0)), 
        fill: "#444444", fillOpacity: 0.3, tip: true,
        title: d => `Count: ${d.length}\nDensity: ${(d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0))).toFixed(3)}`
      }),
      Plot.line(normalCurve, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: () => "Normal Curve", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleX([d3.mean(sample_means)], {stroke: () => "Sampling Distribution Mean", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleX([popMean], {stroke: () => "Population Mean", strokeDasharray: "4,4", strokeWidth: 2, opacity: 0.8})
    ],
    // NEW: Apply the fixed population domain here
    // x: { label: "Sample Mean", tickFormat: ".1f", domain: xLimits }, 
    x: { label: "Sample Mean", tickFormat: ".1f", domain: xLimits2 },
    y: { label: "Density" }
  });

  // --- D. LEGEND & LAYOUT ---
  const myLegend = Plot.legend({
    color: { domain: colorDomain, range: colorRange },
    style: { marginBottom: "10px", fontSize: "14px" }
  });

  return html`
  <div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center;">
    <div style="width: 100%; max-width: 920px; display: flex; justify-content: flex-end;">
      ${myLegend}
    </div>
    <div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 20px; justify-content: center;">
      <div>${popPlot}</div>
      <div>${sampPlot}</div>
    </div>
  </div>`;
}
```

::: {.notes}
As n gets bigger, two things happen

1. Shape gets skinnier (more precise)
As sample size gets bigger, the effect of extreme values goes down (because it's balanced out by other people in the sample). If I get one person who drinks four starbucks coffees per day in a sample of only 4 people, they will have a big impact on our mean. Less so if I have a sample of 100. 
2. Shape gets more Normal (symmetric). This is because as sample size increases, probability of having a sample comprised of a lot of extreme values goes down 

More skewed our population is, the more people we need in our sample to ensure we don't get samples with a high amount of extreme values 
:::

## Recap so far 

::: {.incremental}
<div style="font-size: 130%;">

+ We wanted to use a sample to learn about a population
+ So far, we've taken a lot of different samples of size $n$
+ We saw that the mean of those samples were Normal, as long as $n$ is big enough 
+ **In reality**
  + We only get **one** sample and sample mean ($\bar{X}_n$)
  + We *never* know the true population mean $(\mu)$
  + How far away is our sample mean from the truth?

</div> 
::: 


---

## Central Limit Theorem

<div style="font-size: 130%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ **Central Limit Theorem**: answers this question 

+ As the sample size $n$ increases, the distribution of the sample mean $\bar{X}_n$ approaches a Normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\frac{\sigma^2}{n}$

  + $\mu$: population mean
  + $\sigma^2$: population variance 
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\bar{X}_n  \xrightarrow{d} N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$$
:::

</div>

::: {.notes}
Because we know the distribution of the sample mean, we know how far away our sample is. We know which one is the right one! 

Convergence in distribution: shape approaches shape of Normal
Mathematically: probability rules that govern shape of sample mean = prob rules that govern shape of Normal 
::: 

---

### The Central Limit Theorem


```{r clt plot}
#| cache: true 


pop_mean = mean(caffeine_df$caffeine_mg)
pop_var = var(caffeine_df$caffeine_mg)
se = sqrt(pop_var / 100)

x_min = pop_mean - 3.2 * se; x_max = pop_mean + 3.2 * se
pnormal = 
  ggplot(data = tibble(x = seq(x_min, x_max, 0.01)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = pop_mean, sd = se), linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(y = "Density", x = "Sample mean caffeine intake (mg)", title = "Approximate distribution of sample mean when n = 100",
       subtitle = "By CLT") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(55, 185, 10))

pnormal
```

Let's visualize what the CLT tells us for n = 100

:::

### The Central Limit Theorem


```{r clt plot with annotations}


pop_mean = mean(caffeine_df$caffeine_mg)
pop_var = var(caffeine_df$caffeine_mg)
se = sqrt(pop_var / 100)

x_min = pop_mean - 3.2 * se; x_max = pop_mean + 3.2 * se
pnormal2 = 
  pnormal +
  annotate(geom = "segment",          color = "#444444",
           x = pop_mean + se / 2, xend = pop_mean, y = 0.0025, yend = 0.0025,
          arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "inches"), type = "closed")) +
  annotate(geom = "segment",          color = "#444444",
           x = pop_mean + se / 2, xend = pop_mean + se, y = 0.0025, yend = 0.0025,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "inches"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_labelvline(aes(xintercept = pop_mean), color = "#E69F00", 
                  label = glue::glue("Mean = pop. mean = {round(pop_mean, 0)} mg")) + 
  annotate(geom = "label",
         x = pop_mean + se / 2,
         color = "#444444",
         y = 0.005,
         # Use expression() to wrap the math logic
         label = expression(atop(
           # Top line: Formula
           SD == frac("Population SD", sqrt(n)),
           # Bottom line: Substitution
           phantom(SD) == frac(166, sqrt(100))
         ))) 
pnormal2
```



# The means of our earlier samples were draws from this Normal distribution 

---

### Central Limit Theorem


```{r add sample points}

yval1 = dnorm(vals[1], mean = pop_mean, sd = se)
yval2 = dnorm(vals[2], mean = pop_mean, sd = se)
yval3 = dnorm(vals[3], mean = pop_mean, sd = se)

pnormal2 + 
  annotate(geom = "point", 
           x = vals[1], y = yval1, 
           color = "#CC79A7", size = 5) +
  annotate(geom = "point",
           x = vals[2], y = yval2,

  annotate(geom = "point",
           x = vals[3], y = yval3,
           color = "#0072B2", size = 5)
```

::: {.notes}
In fact, ANY sample mean we get is a draw from this distribution
Therefore, due to facts of the Normal distribution, the sample mean we get is AT MOST 3 SD away from the population mean. Again we can calculate the SD using our sample SD and sample size. You'll notice I'm being a bit hand-wavy here - but next time we'll work through the mechanics of doing this. 
:::

# If we only observe one sample, how can we actually make a statement about the population? 

# Teaser for next time: inference (confidence intervals) 

---

### Using the CLT for inference: confidence intervals 

```{r ci}
#| cache: true

# Let's focus on Sample 1 (Pink)
sample_val = vals[1]
ci_lower = sample_val - 1.96 * se
ci_upper = sample_val + 1.96 * se

# Re-create the plot but make the Truth (Orange Line) faint/dashed to show it's "unknown"
p_inference = 
  ggplot(data = tibble(x = seq(x_min, x_max, 0.01)), aes(x)) +
  # Faint "Truth" distribution
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = pop_mean, sd = se),
  color = "darkgrey", linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0) +
  # The Truth Line (Faint)
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = pop_mean), color = "#E69F00", linetype = "dotted", alpha = 0) +
  # The Sample Dot
  annotate(geom = "point", x = sample_val, y = 0, color = "#CC79A7", size = 5) +
  # The Confidence Interval "Net"
  annotate(geom = "segment", x = ci_lower, xend = ci_upper, y = 0, yend = 0,
           color = "#CC79A7", linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Error Bar whiskers
  annotate(geom = "segment", x = ci_lower, xend = ci_lower, y = -0.001, yend = 0.001,
           color = "#CC79A7", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate(geom = "segment", x = ci_upper, xend = ci_upper, y = -0.001, yend = 0.001,
           color = "#CC79A7", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "", x = "Caffeine (mg)") +
  annotate(geom = "text", x = sample_val, y = 0.001, label = "Lily's Sample Mean", color = "#CC79A7", vjust = 0) +
  annotate(geom = "text", x = pop_mean, y = 0.002, label = "Population Mean", color = "#E69F00", vjust = 0, alpha = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14, color = "#444444")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12))

p_inference
```

---



### Using the CLT for inference: confidence intervals 


```{r ci with theory}

p_inference +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = pop_mean, sd = se),
  color = "darkgrey", linetype = "dashed") +
  # The Truth Line (Faint)
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = pop_mean), color = "#E69F00", linetype = "dotted", alpha = 0.75) + 
  annotate(geom = "text", x = pop_mean, y = 0.005, label = "Population Mean", color = "#E69F00", vjust = 0)

```

::: {.notes}
CI: range of plausible values for the population mean
If we a bunch of different samples of size 100 and calcualted this interval, it would contain the population mean 95% of the time
:::

### Distribution of sample mean: hours worked 

```{ojs}
data2 = FileAttachment("work_df.csv").csv({ typed: true })
sample_values2 = [2, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 200, 500]

viewof sample_index2 = Inputs.range(
  [0, sample_values2.length - 1], // Slide from index 0 to 7
  {
    value: 0, // Index 3 corresponds to value "50" (your previous default)
    step: 1, 
    label: "Sample size:",
    // This makes the label show "50" instead of "3"
    format: i => sample_values2[i] 
  }
)

sample_size2 = sample_values2[sample_index2]

sample_means2 = {
  // Dependency tracking: re-run when these change
  sample_size2;
  
  // Safety check: ensure data is loaded
  if (!data2 || data2.length === 0) return [];
  
  // Safety check: ensure column exists (Case Sensitive!)
  if (typeof data2[0].hrs_worked === "undefined") {
    return ["Error: Column 'hrs_worked' not found in data"];
  }

  const means = [];
  // Create a local copy of the array to shuffle
  // We do this inside the loop or use a specific shuffler to ensure 
  // we are sampling from the full population every time.
  const popArray = Array.from(data2); 

  for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) {
    // 1. Shuffle a clean copy of the population
    // 2. Slice the first n elements (Sampling WITHOUT replacement)
    const sample = d3.shuffle([...popArray]).slice(0, sample_size2);

    // 3. Compute mean
    const m = d3.mean(sample, d => d.hrs_worked);
    means.push(m);
  }

  return means;
}


// 5. CALCULATE NORMAL CURVE (THEORETICAL)
// We now generate the curve based on the Population Parameters, not the sample.
// This shows the Theoretical prediction of the CLT.
normalCurve2 = {
  if (sample_means2.length < 2 || !data2) return [];
  
  // 1. Get Population Statistics
  const popMean = d3.mean(data2, d => d.hrs_worked);
  const popSD = d3.deviation(data2, d => d.hrs_worked);
  
  // 2. Calculate Standard Error (The predicted width of the sampling distribution)
  // Formula: Population SD / sqrt(n)
  const se = popSD / Math.sqrt(sample_size2);

  // 3. Determine range for the curve (centered on popMean)
  const minX = popMean - (4 * se);
  const maxX = popMean + (4 * se);
  
  // Create a smooth grid of X values
  const grid = d3.range(minX, maxX, (maxX - minX) / 200);
  
  // Normal Density Function using Population Mean and Standard Error
  const pdf = (x) => (1 / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))) * Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - popMean) / se, 2));
  
  return grid.map(x => ({x: x, y: pdf(x)}));
}

// 6. PLOT
// 6. SIDE-BY-SIDE PLOTS WITH EXTERNAL LEGEND
{
  // --- A. SETUP VARIABLES ---
  const popMean = d3.mean(data2, d => d.hrs_worked);
  const n = sample_means2.length;
  const bins = d3.bin().thresholds(20)(sample_means2);

  const xLimits = d3.extent(data2, d => d.hrs_worked);

    ],

      Plot.ruleX([d3.mean(sample_means2)], {stroke: () => "Sampling Distribution Mean", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleX([popMean], {stroke: () => "Population Mean", strokeDasharray: "4,4", strokeWidth: 2, opacity: 0.8})
    ],
    // NEW: Apply the fixed population domain here
    x: { label: "Sample Mean", tickFormat: ".1f", domain: xLimits },

  });

  // --- D. LEGEND & LAYOUT ---
  const myLegend = Plot.legend({

  });

  return html`
```

```{ojs}
  // Create a local copy of the array to shuffle
  // We do this inside the loop or use a specific shuffler to ensure 
  // we are sampling from the full population every time.
  const popArray = Array.from(stock); 

  for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) {
    // 1. Shuffle a clean copy of the population
    // 2. Slice the first n elements (Sampling WITHOUT replacement)
    const sample = d3.shuffle([...popArray]).slice(0, sample_size_st);

    // 3. Compute mean
    const m = d3.mean(sample, d => d.sp500_volume);
    means.push(m);
  }

  return means;
}


// 5. CALCULATE NORMAL CURVE (THEORETICAL)
// We now generate the curve based on the Population Parameters, not the sample.
// This shows the Theoretical prediction of the CLT.
normalCurve_stock = {
  if (sample_means_stock.length < 2 || !stock) return [];
  
  // 1. Get Population Statistics
  const popMean = d3.mean(stock, d => d.sp500_volume);
  const popSD = d3.deviation(stock, d => d.sp500_volume);
  
  // 2. Calculate Standard Error (The predicted width of the sampling distribution)
  // Formula: Population SD / sqrt(n)
  const se = popSD / Math.sqrt(sample_size_st);

  // 3. Determine range for the curve (centered on popMean)
  const minX = popMean - (4 * se);
  const maxX = popMean + (4 * se);
  
  // Create a smooth grid of X values
  const grid = d3.range(minX, maxX, (maxX - minX) / 200);
  
  // Normal Density Function using Population Mean and Standard Error
  const pdf = (x) => (1 / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))) * Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - popMean) / se, 2));
  
  return grid.map(x => ({x: x, y: pdf(x)}));
}

// 6. PLOT
// 6. SIDE-BY-SIDE PLOTS WITH EXTERNAL LEGEND
{
  // --- A. SETUP VARIABLES ---
  const popMean = d3.mean(stock, d => d.sp500_volume);
  const n = sample_means_stock.length;
  const bins = d3.bin().thresholds(20)(sample_means_stock);
  
  // NEW: Calculate fixed x-axis limits based on the Population stock
  // This ensures the axis stays constant regardless of sample size
  const xLimits = d3.extent(stock, d => d.sp500_volume);

  // Define colors
  const colorDomain = ["Sampling Distribution Mean", "Population Mean", "Normal Curve"];
  const colorRange = ["black", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"];

  // --- B. POPULATION PLOT (Left) ---
  const popPlot = Plot.plot({
    width: 550,
    height: 500,
    caption: "Population Distribution (Raw Data)",
    marginTop: 40,
    marginLeft: 50,
    marginBottom: 40,
    style: { fontSize: "14px", overflow: "visible" },
    
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(stock, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "sp500_volume", fill: "#444444", fillOpacity: 0.5})),
    ],
    // We explicitly set the domain here too, just to be safe and consistent
    x: { label: "S&P 500 Volume (x10^6)", domain: xLimits }, 
    y: { label: "Count" }
  });

  // --- C. SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION PLOT (Right) ---
  const sampPlot = Plot.plot({
    width: 550,
    height: 500,
    caption: `Sampling Distribution (n=${sample_size_st})`,
    marginTop: 40,
    marginLeft: 50,
    marginBottom: 40,
    style: { fontSize: "14px", overflow: "visible" },
    
    color: {
      domain: colorDomain,
      range: colorRange,
      legend: false
    },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(bins, {
        x1: "x0", x2: "x1", 
        y: d => d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0)), 
        fill: "#444444", fillOpacity: 0.3, tip: true,
        title: d => `Count: ${d.length}\nDensity: ${(d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0))).toFixed(3)}`
      }),
      Plot.line(normalCurve_stock, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: () => "Normal Curve", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleX([d3.mean(sample_means_stock)], {stroke: () => "Sampling Distribution Mean", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleX([popMean], {stroke: () => "Population Mean", strokeDasharray: "4,4", strokeWidth: 2, opacity: 0.8})
    ],
    // NEW: Apply the fixed population domain here
    x: { label: "Sample Mean", tickFormat: ".1f", domain: xLimits }, 
    y: { label: "Density" }
  });

  // --- D. LEGEND & LAYOUT ---
  const myLegend = Plot.legend({
    color: { domain: colorDomain, range: colorRange },
    style: { marginBottom: "10px", fontSize: "14px" }
  });

  return html`
  <div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center;">
    <div style="width: 100%; max-width: 920px; display: flex; justify-content: flex-end;">
      ${myLegend}
    </div>
    <div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 20px; justify-content: center;">
      <div>${popPlot}</div>
      <div>${sampPlot}</div>
    </div>
  </div>`;
}
```

### History: coin flips 

De Moivre and (later) Laplace connect outcomes of coin flips and the Normal distribution 

```{r de moivre laplace}
#| cache: true 

set.seed(345)
coin_flips = tibble(
  flips = 1:10000) %>% 
  rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(
    heads = sum(rbinom(30, size = 1, prob = 0.5))
)
coin_flips %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x= heads)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, color = "black", fill = "#56B4E9")+ 
  labs(x = "# of heads", y = "Count", title = "Number of heads in 30 flips of a coin")
```

::: {.notes}

+ **1733**: Abraham de Moivre realizes that if you flip a coin enough times, the distribution of the number of heads looks like a Normal distribution

+ **1812**: Pierre-Simon Laplace resurrects the idea, showing that you can approximate the Binomial distribution with a Normal distribution

+ **1901**: Aleksandr Lyapunov provides the first rigorous proof of the CLT

+ **1920s**: George Pólya first uses the term *Central Limit Theorem*

:::

## Formal CLT 

Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d) random variables with:
$$E[X_i] = \mu \quad \text{and} \quad 0 < Var(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty$$

<br>

Let $\bar{X}_n$ be the sample mean: $\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$

<br>

As the sample size $n$ approaches infinity, the distribution of the sample mean converges to a Normal distribution:

$$\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{d} N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$$

---

## What assumptions do we need for CLT? 



<div style="font-size: 115%;">

+ **Independence**: the value of one observation must not influence the value of another
  + Violation: siblings, household members, eyes
  
+ **Identically distributed**: all observations come from the same underlying population 
  + Violation: sample from U.S. and Europe 

+ **Finite mean and  variance**: the underlying population must have a defined mean and variance
  + Violation: some theoretical distributions (e.g., Cauchy) where the CLT never applies; not common in real data
  
</div>
